questions.q: Kabir brings a magnet near four things from his desk, one by one: a wooden ruler, an iron key, a rubber eraser and a glass marble. Which statement about his results is correct?
questions.a: Only the iron key sticks; it alone is magnetic here
o: Only the iron key sticks; it alone is magnetic here
The key and the marble stick, since both are hard and shiny
All four stick, since a magnet pulls every solid object
None of them sticks, since magnets only pull other magnets

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: A coin that is pulled towards a magnet could be made of nickel rather than iron.
Statement 2: A spoon made by mixing iron with another metal is sure to be attracted towards a magnet.
Statement 3: A rubber eraser with a small iron clip pushed into it will be pulled towards a magnet.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 only
o: Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 3 only
All three statements

questions.q: A metal strip from a broken toy sticks firmly to a magnet. Pradeep says, 'So the strip must be made of iron.' Which is the best reply?
questions.a: Not necessarily; nickel, cobalt and some of their mixes are attracted too
o: Not necessarily; nickel, cobalt and some of their mixes are attracted too
Yes; iron is the only metal that a magnet can ever attract towards itself
No; it must be cobalt, because iron sticks only to a very large magnet
Yes; nickel and cobalt are metals that are never attracted by a magnet

questions.q: Ritika says, 'Every shiny object is a magnetic material.' Which one observation would show that her idea is wrong?
questions.a: A shiny glass marble does not stick to the magnet
o: A shiny glass marble does not stick to the magnet
A shiny iron nail sticks firmly to the magnet
A dull wooden block does not stick to the magnet
A dull, rusty iron pin still sticks to the magnet

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A cork with an iron sewing needle pushed through it is pulled towards a magnet, although cork is a non-magnetic material.
Reason (R): A magnet attracts the magnetic material in an object even when that material is joined to a non-magnetic one.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
In a Class 6 activity, eight objects were tested with a magnet: an iron nail, a wooden pencil, a rubber eraser, a nickel strip, a glass marble, a plastic scale, a cobalt piece and a cardboard strip. Before testing, Riya predicted 'Yes, it will stick' for the iron nail, the glass marble, the nickel strip and the plastic scale, and 'No' for the other four.
(a) How many of the eight objects will actually stick?
(b) How many of Riya's predictions will be wrong?
(c) What percentage of her predictions will be correct?
(d) Riya's rule was 'smooth, shiny things stick', and she called the iron nail, glass marble, nickel strip and plastic scale smooth and shiny. Do her results support the rule? Name one object that fits it and one that breaks it.
questions.a: (a) 3: the iron nail, nickel strip and cobalt piece. (b) 3: the glass marble, the plastic scale (predicted Yes, actually No) and the cobalt piece (predicted No, actually Yes). (c) 5 correct out of 8 = 62.5%. (d) No. The iron nail (or the nickel strip) fits the rule, but the shiny marble and smooth scale did not stick, and the cobalt piece, which she did not call shiny, did stick. What decides is the material: iron, nickel, cobalt and some of their combinations are attracted.
s: (a) 3 objects
(b) 3 wrong predictions
(d) rule not supported: one fitting object and one breaking object named, material decides

questions.q:
Ankit filled the prediction column of his table before testing with a magnet: iron bolt - Yes; wooden pencil - No; glass bangle - Yes; rubber eraser - No.
(a) Which prediction will turn out wrong, and what will he actually observe?
(b) Which of the four objects will he finally list as non-magnetic?
questions.a: (a) The glass bangle: he predicted Yes, but it will not stick to the magnet. (b) The wooden pencil, the glass bangle and the rubber eraser.
s: Part (a): glass bangle identified as the wrong prediction; it is not attracted
Part (b): pencil, bangle and eraser listed as non-magnetic

questions.q: True or False? 'A material is called magnetic only if it is itself a magnet.' Give the verdict and the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. A magnetic material is any material that is attracted towards a magnet; an ordinary iron nail is not a magnet but it is still attracted, so it is a magnetic material.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: magnetic material means attracted towards a magnet, with an example such as an iron nail that is not a magnet

questions.q: In a fishing game at the class fair, each paper fish has a small clip at its mouth, and the fishing rod ends in a magnet. Arun is making new fish. Which clip would NOT let a fish be caught?
questions.a: A clip made of hard plastic
o: A clip made of hard plastic
A clip made of thin iron wire
A clip made of nickel
A clip made of cobalt

questions.q: Sonu brings a magnet near a cork, a rubber band, a piece of cobalt, a glass bead and a wooden spoon. The number of these five objects that stick to the magnet is ___.

Meera tests three kitchen objects with a magnet: a steel spoon is pulled towards it, a sheet of aluminium foil is not, and a brass key is not.
(a) Classify the three as magnetic or non-magnetic materials, saying what decided each one.
(b) She bends the steel spoon and scratches it. Predict whether it will still be attracted, and give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Steel spoon: magnetic, because it was attracted towards the magnet. Aluminium foil and brass key: non-magnetic, because they were not attracted. The test result decides it, not the fact that all three are metals. (b) Yes. Whether an object is attracted depends on the material it is made of; bending or scratching the spoon does not change its material, so it is still attracted.
s: Part (a): spoon magnetic, foil and key non-magnetic, decided by whether each was attracted
Part (b): still attracted, because the material and not the shape decides

questions.q: Tanvi says, 'Iron is magnetic, so any object made of metal will stick to a magnet. There is no need to test metal objects.' Check her claim.
questions.a: No. The chapter names iron, nickel and cobalt as magnetic metals and says only some of their combinations with other metals are attracted. Being a metal is therefore not enough to be sure, so each metal object still has to be tested with the magnet.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Reason: only iron, nickel, cobalt and some of their combinations are named as magnetic
Conclusion: metal objects must still be tested

questions.q: Gita finds that an iron nail sticks firmly to a magnet. Yet when she touches the same nail to a heap of steel pins, not one pin clings to it. What does this show?
questions.a: The nail is a magnetic material but is not itself a magnet
o: The nail is a magnetic material but is not itself a magnet
The nail is non-magnetic, since it picks up no pins at all
Steel pins are non-magnetic, so nothing can ever lift them
The nail is a magnet that only attracts much heavier objects

questions.q:
Match each observation in Column I with what it shows in Column II.
Column I: 1. A nail sticks to a magnet but picks up no pins by itself  2. A bangle shows no pull at all when a magnet is brought near  3. A dark stone dug up from a hillside pulls iron filings to itself  4. A factory-made sticker holds itself up on a steel cupboard and picks up pins
Column II: a. A naturally occurring magnet  b. An artificial magnet  c. A magnetic material that is not itself a magnet  d. A non-magnetic material

A kabadiwala in Kochi sorts one 50 kg heap of mixed scrap every day: 18 kg of iron pieces, 12 kg of plastic, 8 kg of rubber and 12 kg of wood. At present a helper sorts the whole heap by hand for Rs 400 a day. If he buys a large magnet for Rs 1,500, the helper will be needed for only half a day, at Rs 200.
(a) Which part of the heap can the magnet lift out, and why only that part?
(b) How many kilograms will still need hand sorting after the magnet has done its work, and why can the magnet not help with them?
(c) After how many whole days will the money saved on wages first cover the magnet's price?
(d) He plans to keep trading this way for at least a month. Should he buy the magnet, and can he then let the helper go altogether? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Only the 18 kg of iron pieces, because iron is the one magnetic material in the heap. (b) 12 + 8 + 12 = 32 kg of plastic, rubber and wood; all three are non-magnetic, so the magnet cannot pull any of them out or tell them apart. (c) He saves Rs 400 - Rs 200 = Rs 200 a day; Rs 1,500 / Rs 200 = 7.5, so the savings first cover the price after 8 days. (d) Yes, he should buy the magnet: it pays for itself in 8 days, well inside a month. But he cannot let the helper go, because the 32 kg of non-magnetic plastic, rubber and wood must still be sorted from each other by hand.
s: (a) iron pieces only, the one magnetic material
(b) 32 kg of non-magnetic material, which the magnet cannot sort
(c) Rs 200 saved a day, so 8 days
(d) buy the magnet but keep the helper for the non-magnetic sorting

questions.q:
Reshma's pencil box has a magnet on the box and a metal strip on the lid, which keeps it shut.
(a) The strip is a plain metal strip, not a magnet. Why must it still be made of a magnetic material?
(b) If her brother replaces the strip with a rubber strip of the same size, what will happen to the lid, and why?
questions.a: (a) The magnet holds the lid only if the strip is attracted towards it, and only magnetic materials are attracted. (b) The lid will not stay shut, because rubber is non-magnetic and is not attracted by the magnet.
s: Part (a): the strip must be attracted, which only a magnetic material is
Part (b): lid no longer stays shut, because rubber is non-magnetic

questions.q:
A craft-shop drawer spills on the floor: steel pins, nickel buttons, glass beads, wooden beads and rubber bands are all mixed together. The owner wants five separate heaps and has one magnet and her hands.
(a) Which items will the magnet pick up when it is swept over the heap?
(b) Which items will stay on the floor, and why?
(c) Why can the magnet not separate the steel pins from the nickel buttons?
(d) Why can it not separate the glass beads from the wooden beads either?
(e) Her helper suggests picking out every steel pin by hand first and only then using the magnet. Is that a better order than sweeping with the magnet first? Justify.
questions.a: (a) The steel pins and the nickel buttons, since steel and nickel are attracted by a magnet. (b) The glass beads, wooden beads and rubber bands, because glass, wood and rubber are non-magnetic. (c) Both are attracted, so the magnet lifts them together; it can pull out what is magnetic but cannot tell two magnetic materials apart. (d) Neither is attracted, so the magnet leaves both behind together. (e) No. Sweeping with the magnet first pulls out all the pins and buttons in one go and leaves only two smaller hand jobs (pins from buttons, and the three non-magnetic items from each other). Picking every pin by hand first does the slowest job without the magnet's help, and the magnet would still have to be used afterwards for the buttons.
s: (a) steel pins and nickel buttons
(b) glass, wooden beads and rubber bands stay, being non-magnetic
(c) both pins and buttons are attracted, so they come up together
(d) neither kind of bead is attracted, so both stay together
(e) magnet first is better, justified by the work it saves

questions.q:
A mechanic repairing a ceiling fan keeps dropping its small steel screws, which roll under a cupboard.
(a) How can a magnet help her hold the screws while she works and also get back the ones that rolled away?
(b) The fan also has a few plastic screws. Will the magnet help with them? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) She can keep the steel screws stuck to a magnet on her table while she works, and sweep a magnet (tied to a stick) under the cupboard to pick up the fallen ones, because steel is attracted by a magnet. (b) No. Plastic is a non-magnetic material, so the magnet will not attract the plastic screws; she must pick those up by hand.
s: Part (a): steel screws held and recovered with a magnet, because steel is attracted
Part (b): no help with plastic screws, because plastic is non-magnetic

questions.q: Write a short real-life situation (two or three lines) in which using a magnet to separate magnetic from non-magnetic materials solves a problem. Name what the magnet picks up and what it leaves behind.
questions.a: E.g. At a school fair, a box of iron drawing pins spills into a tray of sawdust used for a game. A volunteer moves a magnet over the sawdust: the iron pins cling to the magnet and the sawdust (wood) stays in the tray, because iron is magnetic and wood is not.
s: A believable situation with a problem to solve
A magnetic item named that the magnet lifts
A non-magnetic item named that stays behind, with the reason

questions.q:
Four metal washers, W, X, Y and Z, look exactly alike. When each is brought near a magnet, W and Y are pulled towards it, while X and Z are not.
(a) Which washers are made of magnetic materials?
(b) Can you be sure that washer W is made of iron? Give a reason.
(c) The seller says all four washers are made of the same metal. Use the results to judge his statement.
questions.a: (a) W and Y. (b) No. Iron is magnetic, but nickel, cobalt and some of their combinations with other metals are also attracted, so W could be made of any of these. (c) He is wrong. Objects made of the same material behave the same way with a magnet; since two washers were attracted and two were not, the washers are made of at least two different materials.
s: Part (a): W and Y
Part (b): not sure, since nickel, cobalt and some combinations are also attracted
Part (c): seller wrong, because one material would give one result for all four

questions.q: A wooden thread spool does not stick to a magnet. Jaya says, 'It does not stick because it is too light.' Varun says, 'It does not stick because wood is not attracted by a magnet.' Whose reason is correct? Support your answer with one observation from a magnet test.
questions.a: Varun's. Being light does not decide it: a light iron pin or iron filings stick to a magnet, but a light spool does not, because wood is a non-magnetic material.
s: Varun's reason chosen
Counter-example: light iron pins or filings are attracted, so material, not weight, decides

questions.q:
A school wants a notice board on which papers are held by small magnets instead of pins. The choices are: an iron-sheet board for Rs 1,250, a wooden board for Rs 800, a plastic board for Rs 650, and a cardboard board for Rs 200. A carpenter also offers to glue an iron strip (Rs 180) along the top edge of the wooden board. The school can spend at most Rs 1,000.
(a) Which of the four boards will hold the magnets anywhere on the surface, and why?
(b) Why will the other three not work on their own?
(c) What would the wooden board with the iron strip cost?
(d) Where on that board would the magnets hold papers?
(e) Which board should the school buy? Justify using your answers.
questions.a: (a) The iron-sheet board, because iron is a magnetic material and attracts the magnets everywhere. (b) Wood, plastic and cardboard are non-magnetic, so the magnets are not attracted. (c) Rs 800 + Rs 180 = Rs 980. (d) Only along the top edge where the iron strip is. (e) The wooden board with the iron strip. The iron-sheet board (Rs 1,250) is over the Rs 1,000 limit; the plastic, cardboard and plain wooden boards fit the budget but cannot hold the magnets at all; the strip board costs Rs 980, inside the limit, even though papers can be held only along its top edge.
s: (a) iron-sheet board, iron is magnetic
(b) wood, plastic, cardboard are non-magnetic
(d) only along the iron strip
(e) strip board chosen: iron-sheet board over budget, the cheaper boards non-magnetic

questions.q: Atharv rolls a bar magnet through a heap of steel U-clips and writes down the clips sticking at three spots: 3, 14 and 12. He forgets to note which count belongs to which spot. Which conclusion is correct?
questions.a: The spot with 3 clips is the middle; the other two are the ends
o: The spot with 3 clips is the middle; the other two are the ends
The spot with 14 clips is the middle, since it held the most
The spot with 12 clips is the middle, as 12 lies in between
None of them is the middle, since a magnet attracts evenly

questions.q: Arjun thinks a longer bar magnet must have more poles. He lays a 5 cm bar magnet and a 15 cm bar magnet on iron filings spread on paper and taps the paper. What will he see?
questions.a: Two thick clusters on each magnet, near its two ends
o: Two thick clusters on each magnet, near its two ends
Two clusters on the short one, three or more on the long one
Filings spread evenly along the whole of the long magnet
Thick clusters only at the middle of the long magnet

questions.q:
Iron filings are spread on a sheet of paper and a bar magnet with no markings is placed on them. The paper is tapped gently.
(a) Where will most of the filings collect, and what are these places called?
(b) Can this test tell you which end is the North pole? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Near the two ends of the magnet; these are its poles (very few filings stick to the rest). (b) No. Most filings stick at both poles alike, so the filings show where the poles are but not which one is North.
s: Part (a): most filings at the two ends, named as the poles
Part (b): no, because filings cluster at both poles, so North cannot be told apart

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: Iron filings stick in equal amounts all along a bar magnet.
Statement 2: A ring magnet has a North pole and a South pole, just as a bar magnet does.
Statement 3: If one end of a bar magnet is painted blue, its North pole is at the other end.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 only
o: Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 3 only
All three statements

questions.q: Om must pick up steel pins scattered on a carpet using one bar magnet. Which way of holding the magnet will collect the most pins in each sweep?
questions.a: Lying flat, so that both of its ends touch the pins
o: Lying flat, so that both of its ends touch the pins
Standing on one end, so it pushes deeper into the pins
Held so that only the middle of it touches the pins
Any way at all, since every part attracts pins equally

questions.q:
A craft club tested two magnets by dipping each into a tray of steel pins and counting where the pins clung. Bar magnet: end A 15, middle 2, end B 14. U-shaped magnet: tip 1 12, bend 1, tip 2 13. A third magnet, half of a bar magnet broken last year, picked up 8 pins at its old end and 1 at its middle; its broken end was not counted.
(a) Where are the poles of the U-shaped magnet?
(b) What percentage of the bar magnet's pins were at its poles? Round to the nearest whole number.
(c) Roughly how many pins would you expect at the broken end of the half-magnet? Give a reason.
(d) Some pins have spilt into a narrow gap between two floor tiles, where only one pole of a magnet can reach at a time. Which magnet should the club use there? Justify using the counts.
questions.a: (a) At its two tips. (b) 29 of 31 pins, about 94%. (c) About as many as the old end, roughly 8, because the broken end is a pole of the half-magnet (every piece has two poles). (d) The bar magnet. Only one pole can work at a time in the gap, so the best single pole matters: the bar's end A held 15 pins against 13 at the U-shaped magnet's better tip. The U-shaped magnet's advantage, having both poles on the same side, is lost in a narrow gap.
s: (a) the two tips
(b) about 94%
(c) about 8, because the broken end is also a pole
(d) bar magnet, best single pole 15 against 13

questions.q:
Leela wants to find out whether all parts of a bar magnet attract magnetic materials equally. Her plan:
Step 1: Hold the bar magnet upright by its top end and dip only its lower end into a box of iron filings.
Step 2: Lift it out and note that filings cling thickly at the lower end.
Step 3: Conclude, 'Only one end of a magnet attracts; its top end and its middle do not.'
(a) What is wrong with Step 1, and how should she set up the test instead?
(b) Why does her conclusion in Step 3 not follow from what she saw?
(c) Predict what the corrected test will show.
(d) She has no more filings, only a box of steel pins. How can she show the same result in numbers, and what pattern of counts should she expect?
(e) Which part of her observation in Step 2 was still correct, and what does it tell her about the lower end?
questions.a: (a) Only the lower end touched the filings, so the top end and the middle were never tested. She should spread the filings on a sheet of paper, lay the magnet flat on them so every part touches, and tap the paper. (b) The top end and the middle did not attract because they never touched the filings, not because they cannot attract; an untested part cannot be said to attract nothing. (c) Most filings will stick near both ends and very few along the middle. (d) Lay the magnet flat in the pins, lift it, and count the pins at end 1, at the middle and at end 2: she should find large counts at both ends and only a few at the middle. (e) Filings clinging thickly at the lower end was a correct observation: that end is one of the magnet's poles, where the attraction is strongest.
s: (a) only one end was tested; lay the magnet flat on spread filings and tap
(b) the other parts were untested, so no conclusion about them
(c) most filings at both ends, few at the middle
(d) count pins at end, middle, end; large-small-large pattern
(e) the lower end is a pole, where attraction is strongest

questions.q: A school kit has 5 bar magnets, 2 U-shaped magnets and 3 ring magnets. Asha paints a red patch on every North pole in the kit. The number of red patches she paints is ___.
True or False? 'A spherical magnet has no poles, because a ball has no ends.' Give the verdict and the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Magnets are made in many shapes, including spherical ones, and every magnet has a North pole and a South pole; poles always occur in pairs, whatever the shape.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: a spherical magnet also has a North and a South pole, since poles occur in pairs in every shape

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Steel pins cling to a U-shaped magnet mostly at its curved bend, because the bend is the thickest part of the magnet.
Reason (R): Most iron filings stick to the poles of a magnet of any shape.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q: Dinesh's bar magnet is painted blue at one end. The paint at its other end has peeled off completely. What is the peeled end?
questions.a: A North pole, as blue paint marks the South pole
o: A North pole, as blue paint marks the South pole
A South pole too, as both ends of a bar always match
No pole at all, as its paint has come off
Not a pole until it is painted again

questions.q: Kunal wants a magnet with only a North pole for a game. He says, 'I will keep cutting a long magnet until the North end comes off on its own.' Show that his plan cannot work.
questions.a: Each time he breaks the magnet, every piece becomes a complete magnet with a North and a South pole. The piece carrying the old North end gets a new South pole at its broken end. Since North and South poles always exist in pairs, even in the smallest piece, a single North pole can never be obtained.
s: Every broken piece is a complete magnet with two poles
The piece with the old North end gets a new South pole at the break
Poles always come in pairs, so a single pole cannot be obtained

questions.q:
Ravi's bar magnet is painted red at one end. Another magnet in the same kit has a white dot at one end and red paint at its other end.
(a) Which pole is the red end of Ravi's magnet?
(b) What is wrong with the markings on the second magnet? Use what the chapter says about poles.
questions.a: (a) The North pole: the North pole of a magnet is sometimes painted red. (b) A white dot also marks a North pole, so both ends of the second magnet are marked North. A magnet always has one North pole and one South pole, so one of its markings must be wrong.
s: Part (a): the red end is the North pole
Part (b): both ends marked North, impossible since a magnet has one North and one South pole

questions.q:
Match each observation or marking in Column I with what it tells us in Column II.
Column I: 1. A bar magnet has a white dot at one end  2. A heap of filings clings thickly at the two ends of a bar magnet  3. A lodestone picks up filings at two regions  4. Only a few filings cling to the middle of a bar magnet
Column II: a. Poles are where the attraction is strongest  b. That end is the North pole  c. The middle of a magnet attracts very weakly  d. A natural magnet also has two poles

A science club has three magnets whose labels are lost: K is an irregular lump, L is a bar and M is U-shaped. One of them is believed to be a lodestone. The pins that clung to each were counted.
K: 9 at one region, 10 at another region, 1 elsewhere.
L: 16 at end A, 3 at the middle, 15 at end B.
M: 11 at tip 1, 2 at the bend, 12 at tip 2.
(a) How many poles does each magnet have, and where are they?
(b) Why does this fit what the chapter says about poles?
(c) How many pins did each magnet hold in all?
(d) Ravi says, 'K held the fewest pins, so K must be the lodestone.' Judge his reasoning.
(e) Can the club decide from these counts which magnet is the lodestone? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Each has two poles: K at the two regions holding 9 and 10 pins, L at ends A and B, M at its two tips. (b) The chapter says most filings stick to the poles of a magnet of any shape and that poles always occur in pairs; it makes no exception for natural magnets. (c) K: 9 + 10 + 1 = 20; L: 16 + 3 + 15 = 34; M: 11 + 2 + 12 = 25. (d) His reasoning does not hold: nothing in the chapter links the number of pins a magnet holds to whether it is natural or artificial, so holding the fewest pins does not show that K is a lodestone. (e) No. All three show the same pattern, two poles with very few pins elsewhere, so the counts cannot tell a natural magnet from an artificial one; the club would need a record of where each magnet came from.
s: (a) two poles each, located correctly
(b) poles of a magnet of any shape, always in pairs
(c) totals 20, 34 and 25
(d) pin count does not show natural or artificial
(e) cannot be decided from the counts, with reason

questions.q:
Ira holds a steel pin against one end of a bar magnet and slides it slowly along the magnet to the other end, keeping it touching all the way.
(a) Where along the magnet will the pin cling most firmly?
(b) Where would you expect the pin to hold on least firmly, and what does that tell you about that part of the magnet?
questions.a: (a) Near each of the two ends, the poles, where most iron filings stick, that is, where the attraction is strongest. (b) Near the middle. Very few iron filings stick there, so the middle attracts magnetic materials only weakly; it is not a pole. (An answer that the pin may not stay at the middle at all is also correct.)
s: Part (a): most firmly near the two ends, the poles
Part (b): least firmly at the middle, which attracts only weakly

questions.q: An online shop advertises a 'North-only magnet' that has a North pole but no South pole. What should a buyer conclude?
questions.a: The claim cannot be true, as every magnet has both poles
o: The claim cannot be true, as every magnet has both poles
It is possible if a long magnet is cut very carefully
It is possible, but only for a spherical magnet
It is possible if the South end is cut off and thrown away

questions.q:
In a pin-lifting contest, four teams each dipped a different magnet into a tray of steel pins once and counted where the pins clung.
Bar magnet: 18 at its two ends, 2 elsewhere.
U-shaped magnet: 16 at its two tips, 1 elsewhere.
Ring magnet: 12 at its two poles, 2 elsewhere.
Disc magnet: 9 at its two poles, 1 elsewhere.
(a) Why did most pins cling at two places on every magnet, whatever its shape?
(b) How many poles do the four magnets have altogether?
(c) For which magnet was the share of its pins held at the poles the highest? Show each percentage, rounded to the nearest whole number.
(d) In the final round, a team scores one point for each pin held at the poles. Which magnet should the school choose for the final? Justify using (c) and the counts.
questions.a: (a) Those two places are the magnet's poles; every magnet, whatever its shape, has a North and a South pole, and most pins stick at the poles. (b) 4 x 2 = 8 poles. (c) Bar 18/20 = 90%; U-shaped 16/17 = 94%; ring 12/14 = 86%; disc 9/10 = 90%. The U-shaped magnet has the highest share. (d) The bar magnet. Points are given for the number of pins at the poles, not the share: the bar held 18 there, more than the U-shaped magnet's 16, even though the U-shaped magnet's share was higher.
s: (a) the two places are the poles, present in every shape
(b) 8 poles
(c) 90%, 94%, 86%, 90%; U-shaped highest
(d) bar magnet, because the score counts pins (18 against 16), not the share

questions.q: Sunil says, 'The middle of a bar magnet hardly attracts anything, so it is not really part of the magnet. If I cut the middle out, I will be left with two end pieces that have only one pole each.' Check his claim.
questions.a: Partly right. His observation is correct: very few iron filings stick to the middle of a bar magnet, so the middle attracts only weakly. His conclusion is wrong: when a magnet is broken, North and South poles always exist in pairs even in the smallest piece, so each end piece will be a complete magnet with two poles.
s: Verdict: partly right
Correct part: very few filings stick at the middle, so it attracts weakly
Wrong part: each piece has a pair of poles, so no single-pole piece is left

questions.q:
Priya wants to find the poles of a bar magnet but has no iron filings, so she spreads sawdust on a sheet of paper and lays the magnet on it.
(a) What will she see, and why?
(b) What could she take from a sewing kit instead, and what result would show her where the poles are?
questions.a: (a) No sawdust sticks anywhere on the magnet, because sawdust is wood, a non-magnetic material, so the test shows nothing about the poles. (b) Steel pins (or iron pins), which are magnetic: when the magnet is laid on them and lifted, most pins cling near its two ends, which are the poles, and very few cling to the middle.
s: Part (a): nothing sticks, since sawdust is non-magnetic
Part (b): steel pins used; most cling near the two ends, the poles

questions.q: Neha claims, 'A ring magnet from a toy and a lodestone in a museum are very different, yet each of them has exactly two poles.' Check her claim.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. A ring magnet is an artificial magnet and a lodestone is a naturally occurring magnet, so they differ in origin and shape. But every magnet, natural or artificial and of any shape, has a North and a South pole, which always occur in pairs.
s: Verdict: the claim is correct
The difference: artificial ring magnet versus natural lodestone
Reason: every magnet of any shape or origin has a pair of poles

questions.q:
Three unmarked bars, P, Q and R, were each hung freely by a thread at the middle and pushed gently four times. Where end 1 of each bar pointed after it came to rest was recorded.
P: north, north, north, north.
Q: east, north-east, south, west.
R: south, south, south, south.
(a) Which bars behave as magnets?
(b) Which end of R is its North-seeking pole?
(c) In what percentage of Q's trials did Q come to rest along the north-south line?
(d) Mina says that one trial for each bar would have been enough. Use Q's record to judge her suggestion.
questions.a: (a) P and R. (b) End 2, because end 1 points south every time. (c) 1 of 4 trials (the third, end 1 pointing south) = 25%. (d) One trial is not enough: if only Q's third trial had been done, Q would have looked like a magnet. Repeating the test shows Q settles in different directions, so it is not a magnet.
s: (a) P and R
(b) end 2 of R
(d) judgement using Q's third trial to show why repeats are needed

questions.q: Diya's freely hung bar magnet comes to rest along the same line every time she pushes it. She now wants to walk towards the east. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: East lies along a line at right angles to the resting line
o: East lies along a line at right angles to the resting line
East lies straight along the resting line, at the red-painted end
East cannot be worked out once the magnet is at rest
East lies in whichever direction the thread was twisted

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A bar magnet hung freely by a thread comes to rest along the north-south direction.
Reason (R): Most iron filings stick near the two ends of a bar magnet.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Sameer hangs an unmarked metal bar from its middle. It stops facing east-west the first time, north-east the second time and north-south the third time. What should he conclude?
questions.a: It is not a magnet; it does not settle in one direction
o: It is not a magnet; it does not settle in one direction
It is a magnet, as it pointed north-south on one of the tries
It is a magnet whose poles keep changing with each push
It is a magnet, but the thread is tied at the wrong end

questions.q: True or False? 'Two bar magnets hung freely from threads at opposite ends of a large playground will come to rest parallel to each other.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Each freely suspended magnet comes to rest along the north-south direction, because the Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet. So both magnets lie along north-south lines, which run the same way and are parallel, however far apart the magnets are.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: each rests north-south because the Earth behaves like a giant magnet, so the two lines are parallel

questions.q:
A bar magnet is hung by a thread tied at its middle and allowed to come to rest.
Statement 1: The end that comes to rest pointing north is called the North-seeking pole.
Statement 2: It comes to rest along north-south because the thread is tied at its middle.
Statement 3: Each time the magnet is given a gentle push, it settles along a different line.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 only
o: Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only

questions.q: A wooden toy fish is hung by a thread tied at its middle. However it is twisted and let go, it comes to rest with its mouth pointing north and its tail pointing south. What is the best explanation?
questions.a: A magnet is hidden inside it, lying from mouth to tail
o: A magnet is hidden inside it, lying from mouth to tail
Wood always comes to rest along the north-south line
The thread untwists to the same position every time
Its heavier mouth end is pulled north by the Earth

questions.q:
Asha's bar magnet is sealed inside a plastic pen case, so she cannot see or mark its ends. She has no other magnet and no compass, but she knows which way is north in her room.
(a) How can she find which end of the pen holds the magnet's North pole?
(b) How can she be sure the result was not just chance?
questions.a: (a) Hang the pen by a thread tied at its middle, adjusted till it hangs level and can turn freely; when it comes to rest, the end of the pen pointing north holds the magnet's North pole. (b) Push it gently and let it come to rest again a few times; if the same end points north every time, the result is not chance.
s: Part (a): hang the pen freely from the middle; the end pointing north holds the North pole
Part (b): repeat several times and check the same end points north

questions.q: Gopal says, 'A suspended magnet points north-south because the Earth behaves like a giant magnet. So any metal bar, if I hang it freely, will also point north-south.' Check his claim.
questions.a: Partly right. The first part is correct: the chapter says a freely suspended magnet rests north-south because the Earth behaves like a giant magnet. The second part is wrong: an iron bar hung freely can rest along any direction; only magnets settle along north-south.
s: Verdict: partly right
Correct part: Earth behaves like a giant magnet, so a suspended magnet rests north-south
Wrong part: a plain iron bar can rest in any direction; only a magnet settles north-south

questions.q: Mili pushes a freely hung, level bar gently five times to test whether it is a magnet. If the bar is a magnet, the number of the five trials in which it comes to rest along the north-south line will be ___.

Tara hangs a bar magnet from a thread in her hostel courtyard. Each time it comes to rest, end A points towards the main gate and end B towards the water tank. The warden tells her the water tank is due south of the gate. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: End A is the magnet's North-seeking pole
o: End A is the magnet's North-seeking pole
End B is the magnet's North-seeking pole
The line from gate to tank runs east-west
Nothing can be said until the Sun rises

questions.q:
Meera ties the thread close to one end of a bar magnet. The magnet hangs tilted, and its lower end rests against the table top.
(a) Why may it not come to rest along north-south?
(b) She re-ties the thread at the middle, but the magnet still hangs slightly tilted. What should she do next, and how will she know the set-up now works?
questions.a: (a) The magnet cannot rotate freely: its lower end rubs against the table, so it stops wherever it happens to be held. (b) Move the thread a little at a time until the magnet is balanced horizontally and hangs clear of the table. Then give it a gentle push a few times: if it comes back to rest along the same line every time, the set-up works.
s: Part (a): it cannot rotate freely while tilted and touching the table
Part (b): adjust the thread till it is balanced horizontally, then check it returns to the same line after gentle pushes

questions.q:
Priya must sort three unmarked metal bars, two magnets and one plain iron bar, using only thread. She knows which way is north in the classroom. Her plan is:
Step 1: Tie the thread near one end of each bar.
Step 2: Let each bar come to rest once and note where it points.
Step 3: Any bar that points north-south is a magnet.
Step 4: Mark the end that points north on each magnet as its North pole.
Find the faults in her plan, correct each one and say why the correction matters. Then say what result will single out the iron bar.
questions.a: Step 1 is faulty: the thread must be tied at the middle and adjusted till the bar is balanced horizontally, so that the bar can rotate freely. Step 2 is faulty: one rest is not enough; she should give each bar a gentle push several times and see whether it comes to rest along the same line each time. Step 3 is faulty as written: the iron bar could come to rest north-south on a single try by chance, so a bar counts as a magnet only if it rests north-south every time. Step 4 is correct once the earlier steps are fixed: the end that points north every time is the North-seeking, or North, pole. The iron bar is the one that comes to rest along different directions on different pushes.
s: Step 1 corrected: tie at the middle, balanced horizontally, to rotate freely
Step 2 corrected: repeat after gentle pushes
Step 3 corrected: north-south every time, since iron may stop there once by chance
Step 4 kept: the end pointing north every time is the North pole
Iron bar: rests in different directions on different pushes

questions.q: Neel says, 'My hung magnet rests north-south only because of the steel cupboards beside it in my classroom.' Which test would best check his idea?
questions.a: Hang it in the middle of an open field, far from the cupboards
o: Hang it in the middle of an open field, far from the cupboards
Hang it even closer to the steel cupboards and watch it carefully
Hang a plain iron bar beside the cupboards in its place
Hang it from a thicker thread at the very same spot

questions.q:
Ravi hangs an unmarked bar magnet freely in a new town and marks on the floor the line it comes to rest along.
(a) How can he use the Sun to check roughly which way his line runs?
(b) One evening his line seems to point straight at the setting Sun. What should he suspect, and why?
questions.a: (a) He can notice where the Sun rises or sets, which gives an approximate idea of where east or west is; a line along which a magnet rests should run north-south, across the east-west direction, not along it. (b) The setting Sun is roughly in the west, so his line would be running east-west, not north-south. A freely suspended magnet always rests north-south, so he should suspect that the bar was not hanging freely (or is not a magnet), check that it hangs level and clear of everything, and repeat.
s: Part (a): sunrise or sunset gives an approximate east or west, which the north-south line should cross
Part (b): the line looks east-west, so the bar was probably not hanging freely; check and repeat

questions.q:
The school gardener must lay out new vegetable beds that run exactly north-south. He has a bar magnet with unmarked ends and some string, and he hangs the magnet five times. In trials 1, 2, 4 and 5 it hangs level and, after a gentle push, comes to rest along the line from the tap to the tool shed. In trial 3 the string slips towards one end, the magnet hangs tilted with one end touching a wooden stake, and it stops along the line from the tap to the gate. A ready-made compass will arrive only next week. Seeds sown this week give the best crop; sown next week, they still grow but give a smaller crop.
(a) How must the magnet be hung so that its resting line can be used?
(b) Which trial should he not count, and why?
(c) Does he need to know which end of the magnet is the North pole in order to lay out the beds? Explain.
(d) Should he mark out the beds today from his trials, or wait for the compass? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Tied by the string at its middle, adjusted till it hangs level and clear of everything, so that it can turn freely, then left to come to rest. (b) Trial 3. The magnet was tilted and touching the stake, so it could not rotate freely, and where it stopped does not show north-south. The four trials in which it hung freely all agree. (c) No. The beds only have to run along the north-south line, and both ends of the magnet lie on that line; which end points north does not change the line. (d) Mark them today along the tap-to-shed line. Every trial in which the magnet hung freely gave that same line, and a freely suspended magnet always rests north-south; the one odd trial has a known cause. The compass would show the same north-south line a week later, at the cost of a smaller crop. (Had the proper trials disagreed with one another, waiting would have been the safer choice.)
s: (a) hung from the middle, level and free to turn
(b) trial 3 not counted, since the magnet could not turn freely
(c) no, the line is the same whichever end is North
(d) mark today: the four free trials agree and the odd one has a known cause, weighed against the smaller crop

questions.q: A sealed cardboard parcel is hung by a thread tied at its middle so that it hangs level and turns freely. Pushed gently four times, it comes to rest each time with its label end pointing west. Dev says, 'If there were a magnet inside, the label end would point north. So there is no magnet in it.' Check his claim.
questions.a: No. A magnet inside need not lie along the label end. If it lies across the parcel, the parcel turns until the hidden magnet rests along north-south, and the label end then points east or west. What matters is that the parcel comes to rest in the same direction every time, while a plain iron bar, in the chapter's words, can rest along any direction. Settling the same way on all four pushes suggests there is a magnet inside, lying across the parcel.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
A hidden magnet lying across the parcel makes the label end point east or west
Resting the same way every time is the sign of a magnet; iron rests in any direction

questions.q: A hung bar magnet with its North pole painted red comes to rest with the red end pointing north. Ria gently turns it round by hand until the red end faces south, holds it still, and then lets go. What happens next?
questions.a: It swings round and settles with the red end north again
o: It swings round and settles with the red end north again
It stays where it is, with the red end still facing south
It settles east-west, halfway between the two positions
It keeps spinning round and never comes to rest again

questions.q: Write a short situation (two or three lines) in which someone with no compass uses a freely suspended bar magnet, whose North pole is painted red, to find a direction. Then say which end of the magnet tells them north and why the magnet settles that way.
questions.a: E.g. On a cloudy afternoon at a farm near Nashik, Kiran must walk north to the well. She hangs her bar magnet from a string tied at its middle and waits; the red-painted end, the North-seeking pole, comes to rest pointing north each time, so she walks the way it points. The magnet settles north-south because the Earth behaves like a giant magnet.
s: A believable situation where a direction is needed and no compass is at hand
The North-seeking end of the freely hung magnet used to find north
Reason: the Earth behaves like a giant magnet

questions.q:
A group of Class 6 students and their teacher are on a bare hilltop in the Nilgiris at dusk when thick fog rolls in. Their bus is parked due north of the hill. The teacher has a bar magnet with its North pole painted red, and some string, but the strong wind keeps the hanging magnet swinging. The only shelter is a shepherd's hut with closed walls, 25 minutes away down a steep, rocky path; after using the magnet there, the group would have to climb back up before setting off north. The shepherd says the wind sometimes drops within an hour, but on some nights it blows until morning. The Sun will not rise for another 11 hours.
(a) What must happen to the hanging magnet before its direction can be trusted, and why does the wind prevent this?
(b) Once the magnet settles, how will it show them the way to the bus?
(c) Why does the fog not stop the magnet from working, though it hides the sky?
(d) One student suggests waiting on the hilltop for sunrise and using the Sun instead. Give one weakness of this plan, using what the chapter says about the Sun.
(e) Should the group go down to the hut and hang the magnet there, or wait on the hilltop for the wind to drop? Justify, weighing what each choice costs.
questions.a: (a) It must turn freely and come to rest; only a magnet at rest shows the north-south direction. The wind keeps pushing it, so it never comes to rest. (b) It comes to rest along north-south with its red North-seeking end pointing north, which is the way to the bus. (c) The magnet rests north-south because the Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet; this does not depend on seeing the sky. (d) The Sun gives only an approximate idea of where east or west is, it cannot be used for 11 hours, and the fog may still hide it then. (e) Go down to the hut. Waiting costs no walking and might work within an hour, but the wind may blow until morning, leaving the group with no direction at all for up to 11 hours in the cold and dark. The hut costs about 50 minutes of walking (25 down and 25 back up) on a rough path, but inside its walls the magnet can come to rest, so it is the only choice certain to give the way north.
s: (a) must come to rest; the wind keeps it moving
(b) red North-seeking end points north, towards the bus
(c) works because the Earth behaves like a giant magnet
(d) the Sun gives only an approximate direction, and not for 11 hours
(e) hut chosen: about 50 minutes of walking weighed against a wait that may last till morning

questions.q:
Kavi hangs a bar magnet freely over a sheet of paper, marks the points under its two ends when it comes to rest, and joins them. The line runs from the door end of the room towards the window end.
(a) The door is on the south side of the room. Under which end of the line is the magnet's North-seeking pole?
(b) His sister turns the sheet of paper round so that the drawn line points a different way, then hangs the magnet over it again. Will the magnet now come to rest along the drawn line? Explain.
questions.a: (a) The window end, because the door end is towards the south and the North-seeking pole points north. (b) No. The magnet comes to rest along the north-south direction, whatever the paper does. The drawn line was only a record of that direction; turning the paper turns the record away from north-south, but the magnet still settles north-south, so it no longer lies along the line.
s: Part (a): the window end
Part (b): no; the magnet still rests north-south, and the turned line is only a record

questions.q: Kavya places a compass on her desk. When the needle stops, its red end lies over the 'E' mark on the dial. What should she do before reading any direction?
questions.a: Turn the box until the 'N' mark lies under the red end
o: Turn the box until the 'N' mark lies under the red end
Push the needle round with a finger until it points at 'N'
Read east from the red end, since the needle is set
Shake the compass until the needle points at 'N'

questions.q: True or False? 'A needle compass made by floating a magnetised needle on a cork in water can show north-south even though it has no dial.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The magnetised needle is a magnet that can turn freely on the floating cork, so it comes to rest along north-south. A dial only helps to read the other directions once it is lined up with the needle; it is not what makes the needle point north-south.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: a freely turning magnetised needle rests north-south; the dial only helps read other directions

questions.q: To magnetise a sewing needle, Rohit rubs one pole of a bar magnet back and forth along it 40 times. Which instruction of the activity has he ignored?
questions.a: Move the same pole one way only, lifting it at the end
o: Move the same pole one way only, lifting it at the end
Use both poles of the magnet, one after the other
Stroke the needle at least 100 times, not 40 times
Hold the needle under water while stroking it every time

questions.q:
Match each fault in Column I with its effect in Column II.
Column I: 1. Compass needle glued to the dial  2. Box not turned after the needle has come to rest  3. Red paint worn off the needle  4. Steel pins not attracted by a stroked sewing needle
Column II: a. The needle has not yet become a magnet  b. The needle cannot rotate freely, so it shows no true north-south  c. Directions read off the dial are wrong, though the needle points north-south  d. You cannot tell at a glance which end of the needle points north

Sana has stroked an iron sewing needle with a magnet 35 times. Held over a heap of steel pins, two pins jump up to it; held over a heap of sawdust, it picks up nothing.
(a) Has the needle become a magnet? Which of the two tests tells her?
(b) Her friend says the sawdust result proves the needle is not a magnet. How should Sana reply?
questions.a: (a) Yes. The steel-pin test tells her: the activity says that if pins or iron filings are attracted to the needle, it has become a magnet. (b) The sawdust result proves nothing: sawdust is wood, a non-magnetic material, which no magnet attracts, so even a strong magnet would pick up none of it.
s: Part (a): yes, shown by the steel pins being attracted
Part (b): sawdust is non-magnetic, so it is not attracted even by a magnet

questions.q: In a cheap toy compass, the needle has come off its pin and been glued flat onto the dial instead. What will go wrong when the compass is used?
questions.a: The needle cannot rotate freely, so it points wherever the box is turned
o: The needle cannot rotate freely, so it points wherever the box is turned
The needle still swings round freely, but now it comes to rest east-west
The glue removes the needle's red paint, so north can no longer be read
Nothing goes wrong, because the glued needle is still a small magnet

questions.q:
Assertion (A): After placing a compass down, we gently turn the box until the North and South marks on the dial line up with the needle, and only then read other directions.
Reason (R): The needle turns to point in whichever direction the 'N' mark on the dial is facing.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
Five groups tried to magnetise iron sewing needles and then tested each needle with steel pins. Their notes:
Group 1: one pole, one direction, lifting at the end, 40 strokes; pins attracted.
Group 2: one pole, one direction, lifting at the end, 35 strokes; pins attracted.
Group 3: back and forth along the needle, 40 strokes; no pins attracted.
Group 4: one pole, one direction, lifting at the end, 10 strokes; no pins attracted.
Group 5: one direction, lifting at the end, 40 strokes, but changed to the other pole halfway; no pins attracted.
(a) Which groups followed every instruction of the activity?
(b) For each of Groups 3, 4 and 5, name the instruction that was not followed.
(c) What percentage of the groups have needles ready to go through a cork?
(d) Riya says, 'Group 3's result proves that stroking back and forth can never magnetise a needle.' Can one trial prove this? Explain.
(e) What should Groups 3, 4 and 5 do next, and how will they know they have succeeded?
questions.a: (a) Groups 1 and 2. (b) Group 3: the magnet must move along the needle in one direction only, be lifted at the end and brought back to the starting end. Group 4: the stroke must be repeated at least 30 to 40 times; 10 is too few. Group 5: the same pole must be used for every stroke. (c) 2 of 5 groups = 40%. (d) No. One trial shows only that this needle was not magnetised this time; the chapter gives a method to follow, not a rule about other methods, so a single result cannot prove what will never happen. (e) Repeat the stroking exactly as the activity says (same pole, one direction, lifting and returning to the same end, 30 to 40 times) and test again with steel pins or iron filings; if they are attracted, the needle has become a magnet.
s: (a) Groups 1 and 2
(b) the missed instruction for Groups 3, 4 and 5
(d) one trial cannot prove 'never'; the chapter gives only the method
(e) repeat the method correctly and retest with pins or filings

questions.q: Ishaan holds his compass level on his palm, waits for the needle to rest and turns the box until 'N' lies under the red end. Then, still holding it level, he turns round to face the playground, so the box turns with him. Which is now correct?
questions.a: The needle still points north, but 'N' has moved away from it
o: The needle still points north, but 'N' has moved away from it
The needle has turned round with the box, so 'N' is still under it
The needle now points towards the playground he is facing
The needle stays fixed to the dial, since the box was set

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: If a compass needle rubs against the dial because its pin is bent, the needle may stop in any direction.
Statement 2: A sewing needle stroked correctly 40 times that still lifts no steel pins should not yet be pushed through the cork.
Statement 3: The matsya-yantra could show direction because its magnetised fish-shaped iron piece, kept in a vessel of oil, could turn, much like a needle on a floating cork.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: All three statements
o: All three statements
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 1 only

questions.q:
Raju sets his compass down and at once, while the needle is still swinging, turns the box so that 'N' is under the red end. Then he reads the directions off the dial.
(a) What is wrong with this, and how could it spoil his readings?
(b) What should he do before turning the box?
questions.a: (a) A swinging needle has not yet come to rest along north-south, so the 'N' mark he lines up with it may not face north; every direction he reads off the dial could then be wrong. (b) Leave the compass where he wants to know the directions and wait until the needle comes to rest; only then turn the box gently until the North and South marks line up with the needle.
s: Part (a): the needle is not yet resting north-south, so the dial may be set wrong
Part (b): wait for the needle to rest, then line up N and S with it

questions.q:
Three students' needle compasses failed. Suggest the most likely cause for each and how to fix it.
(a) Asif's needle attracts no steel pins at all.
(b) Bela's needle attracts pins well. She pushed it through the cork close to the cork's bottom face, and when floated the cork stops in a different place each time.
(c) Chirag's needle lifts only a single pin, weakly. His cork floats freely, clear of the bowl's sides, but stops in a different direction every time he turns it.
questions.a: (a) The needle has not become a magnet: most likely a step of the stroking was missed (the same pole, one direction only, lifting at the end and returning to the starting end, 30 to 40 times). Another possible cause is that the needle is not made of iron. Fix: stroke it again correctly and retest with pins. (b) The needle sits under the water, so it is not free to turn; it must be passed through the cork so that it stays above the level of the water. (c) The needle is only weakly magnetised, if at all, since it barely attracts pins; most likely it was stroked too few times or not in one direction. Fix: stroke it 30 to 40 times exactly as the activity says and test with pins before floating it again.
s: Part (a): needle not magnetised, a stroking step missed (or not an iron needle)
Part (b): needle under water, so not free to turn; keep it above the water
Part (c): barely magnetised; restroke 30 to 40 times correctly and retest

questions.q:
In a school treasure hunt, Nikhil sets his compass on a flat stone beside the flagpole. The dial's marks run clockwise in the order N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW. The needle comes to rest with its red end over the 'S' mark. The last clue says the treasure is buried to the north-east of the flagpole.
(a) In which real direction does the red end of the needle point?
(b) Without turning the box, which dial mark is facing real north-east?
(c) Before Nikhil can move, Kabir drops his school bag on the stone with its pencil box, which closes with a magnet clasp, right against the compass, and runs off to the next clue. The needle swings round. Why?
(d) The rules forbid touching another player's bag, and only two minutes are left. Nikhil can carry his compass to the stage steps, the only other flat place, a minute's walk away, wait for the needle to settle and walk back; or he can use the answer to (b), which he worked out before the bag arrived, since the compass box has not been moved. Which should he do? Justify.
questions.a: (a) North. (b) The 'SW' mark. The red end, which points north, lies over 'S', so the dial is turned half way round and every mark faces the opposite of its label; real north-east is faced by the 'SW' mark. (c) The clasp holds a magnet, and the compass needle is itself a magnet, so the nearby magnet attracts or repels its ends and pulls it away from north-south. (d) Use the answer to (b) and walk the way the 'SW' mark faces. That reading was taken while the needle was at rest with no magnet nearby, and the box has not moved since, so the dial still shows the real directions. A fresh reading at the steps would also be correct, but walking there and back and waiting for the needle to settle would use up almost all of the two minutes for an answer he already has.
s: (a) north
(b) the 'SW' mark, since the dial is half a turn round
(c) the clasp magnet acts on the needle, which is itself a magnet
(d) use the earlier reading: taken at rest with no magnet near and the box unmoved, weighed against the time a new reading costs

questions.q: Leela's floating needle compass keeps touching the side of the bowl and stopping in different places. Which change will most likely let it work?
questions.a: Use a wider bowl so the cork can turn freely
o: Use a wider bowl so the cork can turn freely
Push the needle under water so it stays steady
Stroke the needle with both poles, one by one
Tie the cork to the bowl so it cannot drift away

questions.q: A magnetised sewing needle is pushed through a floating cork, and the cork is turned gently five times. Each time it stops, the eye end of the needle points north. The eye end is the needle's ___ pole.
questions.a: North

questions.q: After making her cork compass, Priya rotates the cork gently several times and waits each time for it to stop. Why does she do this, and what result tells her the compass works?
questions.a: To check that the needle settles in the same direction every time and not by chance. If the same end of the needle always points the same way (north-south), the compass works.
s: Purpose: to check it settles the same way each time
Result: the same end always points the same direction

questions.q: Arjun says, 'The matsya-yantra and today's compass work on completely different ideas, so the matsya-yantra was not really a compass at all.' Check his claim.
questions.a: No. Both rely on the same idea: a magnetised iron piece that can turn freely comes to rest along north-south. The matsya-yantra kept its fish-shaped magnet in a vessel of oil, a device the chapter calls similar to the cork compass that floats a needle in water, and Indians used it for navigation at sea long before the modern compass was widespread. Only the build differs, not the idea.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Shared idea: a freely turning magnetised piece settles north-south
Evidence: fish-shaped magnet kept in oil, used for navigation at sea

questions.q:
The school gate is due north of the flagpole. Four groups stand at the flagpole and use compasses to find the direction of the gate. Every dial is marked clockwise N, E, S, W.
Group P: modern compass; waited for the needle to rest, turned the box until 'N' lay under the red end; reported 'north'.
Group Q: modern compass; the needle came to rest with its red end over 'E'; they did not turn the box and read the gate's direction straight off the dial; reported 'east'.
Group R: cork-and-needle compass; the needle sat under the water and the cork kept touching the side of the bowl; reported 'north-west' the first time and 'south' the second.
Group S: modern compass whose red paint had worn off; they lined up 'N' with the wrong end of the needle; reported 'south'.
(a) Which group's report can be trusted, and what did it do that made the reading trustworthy?
(b) Explain how Group Q's mistake made the gate seem to be in the east.
(c) On Group Q's unturned dial, the school well lies beyond the 'N' mark. In which real direction is the well?
(d) Why can Group R's compass not be trusted, and what two changes would fix it?
(e) Why is Group S's answer exactly opposite to the truth, even though their needle did rest along north-south?
questions.a: (a) Group P. It let the needle come to rest along north-south and then turned the box until the North and South marks lined up with the needle, so every mark on its dial faced its real direction. (b) The red end points north and lay over 'E', so on the unturned dial the 'E' mark was facing real north. The gate, being north, lay beyond the 'E' mark, so Group Q read 'east'. (c) West. With the 'E' mark facing north, every mark faces a quarter turn anticlockwise from its label: going clockwise N, E, S, W, the 'N' mark lies a quarter turn anticlockwise from 'E', which in real directions is west. (d) The needle could not turn freely: it was under the water and the cork touched the bowl, so it stopped in different places. Keep the needle above the level of the water, and use a wider bowl (or keep the cork away from the sides) so the cork can turn freely. (e) They lined up 'N' with the end that points south, so the dial was set half a turn round and every direction read off it was the opposite of the real one. The needle was right; only the end used as north was wrong, which is why the north end of a compass needle is usually painted red.
s: (a) Group P, needle at rest and dial lined up with it
(b) the 'E' mark faced north on the unturned dial
(c) west, worked out from the dial order
(d) not free to turn; needle above water and cork clear of the sides
(e) N lined up with the south-pointing end, so the dial was half a turn round

questions.q:
A compass is set down and its needle comes to rest with the red end over the 'W' mark on the dial. The dial's marks run clockwise in the order N, E, S, W.
(a) In which real direction does the red end point?
(b) Before the box is turned, the 'N' mark on the dial points towards a temple. In which real direction is the temple?
questions.a: (a) North, because the red end of a compass needle rests towards north. (b) East. With the red end (true north) over 'W', the dial is turned a quarter round; going clockwise N, E, S, W, the 'N' mark lies a quarter turn clockwise from 'W', which in real directions is east.
s: Part (a): north
Part (b): east, worked out from the dial order

questions.q: Write four short numbered instructions that a Class 5 child could follow to make a needle compass with a cork, a bar magnet, a sewing needle and a bowl of water. Then add one line on how to check that it works.
questions.a: E.g. 1. Lay the needle on a wooden table and put one pole of the magnet on one end. 2. Slide that pole along to the other end, lift it, bring the same pole back to the starting end; do this 30 to 40 times. 3. Check that the needle now attracts steel pins. 4. Push the needle sideways through the cork and float the cork in the bowl, needle above the water. Check: turn the cork gently a few times; the same end should always stop pointing the same way.
s: Stroking with one pole in one direction, 30 to 40 times
Testing with pins and floating on a cork with the needle above water
A check that the same end always points the same way

questions.q:
A Class 6 class of 30 students works in groups of 5 to make floating needle compasses. Each group needs one cork (Rs 5) and one iron sewing needle (Rs 2). Bar magnets cost Rs 85 each and two groups share one magnet. Bowls are borrowed from the laboratory. The teacher's budget is Rs 305.
(a) Why is the needle pushed through a cork rather than dropped straight into the water?
(b) What will the class spend on corks, needles and magnets, and how much of the budget will be left?
(c) Why must each group test its needle with steel pins before pushing it through the cork?
(d) The teacher had hoped to buy a ready-made compass (Rs 95) to check the class's compasses, or spare cork-and-needle sets at Rs 7 a set. What can she actually buy, and how can the class still check its compasses? Justify.
questions.a: (a) The cork keeps the needle floating above the water so that it can turn freely and settle north-south. (b) 6 groups: corks 6 x 5 = Rs 30, needles 6 x 2 = Rs 12, magnets 3 x 85 = Rs 255; total Rs 297, leaving Rs 8. (c) To check that the needle has become a magnet; a needle that is not a magnet will not come to rest along north-south, so the compass would be useless. (d) The compass is out of reach (Rs 95 is far more than the Rs 8 left), so she can buy one spare set for Rs 7, leaving Re 1. The class can still check its compasses against each other: every working needle should come to rest along the same north-south line as the others and return to it each time its cork is turned, which is how a freely turning magnet behaves.
s: (a) cork keeps the needle afloat and free to turn
(b) Rs 297 spent, Rs 8 left
(c) the pin test shows the needle has become a magnet, needed for it to settle north-south
(d) one spare set only, and a check by all needles resting along the same line

questions.q: In a 'hopping frog' toy, ring magnets are glued along a scale so that their upper faces are North, South, North, South in turn. A paper frog with a ring magnet at its base, South face downwards, is slid along just above them. Why does the frog hop?
questions.a: It is pushed up over like poles and pulled down over unlike poles
o: It is pushed up over like poles and pulled down over unlike poles
It is pulled up over every ring, since all magnets attract
It is pushed up over unlike poles and then pulled down over like poles
It hops only because the plastic strip bends as it slides

questions.q: Magnet A, with its poles marked, rests on round pencils. Gautam brings end 1 of an unmarked magnet B near A's North pole, and A rolls away. Then he brings the same end 1 near A's South pole. What will A do?
questions.a: Roll towards B, as end 1 is a North pole
o: Roll towards B, as end 1 is a North pole
Roll away again, as B always pushes A
Stay still, as end 1 has used up its push
Roll away, as end 1 is a South pole

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: A car carrying a plain iron strip will run away from a magnet car if the iron-strip car is turned round.
Statement 2: Magnets in storage are kept in pairs with unlike poles on the same side.
Statement 3: In a stored pair, a piece of soft iron is placed between the two magnets and pieces of wood across their ends.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 only

Statements 1 and 2 only

questions.q:
Three ring magnets are slipped onto an upright pencil. The top ring floats above the middle ring without touching it, while the middle ring rests touching the bottom ring.
(a) What kind of poles face each other between the top and middle rings, and between the middle and bottom rings?
(b) The middle ring is taken off, turned over and slipped back on. Predict what the rings will now do.
questions.a: (a) Top and middle: like poles, which repel, so the top ring floats. Middle and bottom: unlike poles, which attract, so they touch. (b) Turning the middle ring over swaps its two faces. Now unlike poles face the top ring, so the top ring comes down and sticks to the middle ring, and like poles face the bottom ring, so the middle ring (with the top ring on it) floats above the bottom ring.
s: Part (a): like poles between top and middle, unlike between middle and bottom
Part (b): top sticks to middle, and the pair floats above the bottom ring

questions.q: A toy seller has three toy fish, P, Q and R, that look the same. Each has a short metal bar inside: in two fish the bar is a magnet, in one it is plain iron. Which single observation proves for certain that fish Q holds a magnet?
questions.a: Q's nose pushes away the tail of fish P
o: Q's nose pushes away the tail of fish P
Q's nose pulls the tail of fish P closer
Both ends of Q are pulled by one end of R
Q clings firmly to the side of fish R

questions.q:
At the school fair, Reshma's stall has two matchbox cars, car 1 and car 2, each with a bar magnet fixed along its length so that the North pole is at the front of the car. A third car carries only a plain iron strip.
(a) Car 2 is placed behind car 1, so that car 2's front faces car 1's back. What happens when they are brought close?
(b) What happens if instead the backs of the two cars face each other?
(c) What happens whichever end of the iron-strip car is brought near the front of car 1?
(d) Reshma wants car 1 to push another car along the track in front of it without touching it. Which car should she place in front of car 1, and which way round? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Car 2's front is a North pole and car 1's back is a South pole; unlike poles attract, so the cars move towards each other. (b) Both backs are South poles; like poles repel, so the cars move apart. (c) It is attracted either way, since both ends of an iron bar are attracted by both poles of a magnet. (d) Car 2, turned so that its front (North pole) faces car 1's front (North pole): like poles repel, so car 2 is pushed ahead. Facing the other way, car 2 would show its South pole and be pulled back, and the iron-strip car would be pulled whichever way it faced, because iron is never repelled.
s: (a) North facing South: unlike poles attract, cars move together
(b) South facing South: like poles repel, cars move apart
(c) iron strip attracted from either end
(d) car 2 facing car 1 front to front, justified by like poles repelling and iron never repelling

questions.q: Two bar magnets are stored side by side by the chapter's storage rule. If the North pole of the first magnet is at the left, the pole of the second magnet at the left is its ___ pole.
questions.a: South

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A plain iron bar resting on round pencils rolls towards a bar magnet whichever end of the magnet is brought near it.
Reason (R): A magnet can be identified by its property of repulsion.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: End X of an unmarked bar magnet is brought slowly towards the North end of a resting compass needle, and the needle's North end swings away. What will the needle's North end do when the other end, Y, of the same magnet is brought near it instead?
questions.a: Swing closer, as Y is a South pole
o: Swing closer, as Y is a South pole
Swing away again, as both ends are North
Stay still, as only X is a pole
Swing away, as a needle avoids all magnets

questions.q: True or False? 'If one end of a bar makes the North end of a compass needle swing closer, that end must be the South pole of a magnet.' Give the verdict and the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The compass needle is itself a magnet, and a magnet attracts both ends of a plain iron bar. So the needle's North end swings closer to a South pole and also to either end of a plain iron bar. Swinging closer does not prove the end is a South pole of a magnet; only the needle being pushed away would show that the bar is a magnet.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: attraction also happens with plain iron; only repulsion proves a magnet

questions.q:
Car 1 carries a bar magnet with its North pole at the front. Car 2 carries an unmarked bar magnet, and car 3 an unmarked metal bar.
(a) When car 2's front is brought near car 1's front, car 2 is pushed back. What pole is at car 2's front?
(b) Car 3 is brought up to car 1's front, first with one end leading and then with the other, and it is pulled closer both times. What does this tell you about car 3's bar, and why?
questions.a: (a) A North pole, because like poles repel. (b) Car 3's bar is not a magnet; it is a magnetic material such as plain iron. A magnet has a North and a South pole, so with one of its two ends leading, its North pole would have faced car 1's North pole and been pushed away. Being pulled at both ends is how a plain iron bar behaves.
s: Part (a): North, since like poles repel
Part (b): not a magnet, since a magnet would have been repelled with one end leading

questions.q: Two unmarked bars, F and G, push each other away when one end of F is brought near one end of G. Rahul thinks one of them might still be plain iron. Show that this cannot be.
questions.a: If F were plain iron, both its ends would be attracted by both poles of G, so G could never push it away. The same holds if G were iron. Repulsion happens only between two magnets, so both F and G must be magnets.
s: If one bar were iron it would only be attracted, never repelled
This applies whichever bar is assumed to be iron
Repulsion needs two magnets, so both are magnets

questions.q: Shreya says, 'A big magnet always pulls a small magnet towards it, whichever ends face each other.' Which observation would show that she is wrong?
questions.a: A big magnet's North pole pushes away a small magnet's North pole
o: A big magnet's North pole pushes away a small magnet's North pole
A big magnet's North pole pulls in a small magnet's South pole
A big magnet pulls a small iron nail towards it from either of its ends
A small magnet's South pole pulls in a big magnet's North pole

questions.q:
For the fair, Reshma builds a 'magnet train' of four matchbox cars, A, B, C and D, each carrying a bar magnet along its length. The pole at the front of each car is: A North, B South, C North, D South. She puts them in a line on the track, A, then B, then C, then D, all facing the same way, so that the front of A faces the back of B, the front of B faces the back of C, and the front of C faces the back of D.
(a) What pole is at the back of each car?
(b) Which neighbouring pairs of cars will attract and which will repel? Explain.
(c) She wants all four cars to cling together as one train. What is the smallest number of cars she must turn round, and which ones? Explain why fewer will not do.
(d) Kunal says, 'Just turn every car round and they will all cling together.' Check his claim.
(e) She also has a car carrying only a plain iron strip. Where in the finished train could it go so that it clings to its neighbours, and which way round must it face?
questions.a: (a) A South, B North, C South, D North, since each bar magnet has its other pole at the back. (b) All three pairs repel: A's front (North) faces B's back (North), B's front (South) faces C's back (South), and C's front (North) faces D's back (North); each time like poles face each other. (c) Two cars: turn B and D round (turning A and C instead also works). Then North faces South at every gap, so every pair attracts. Turning one car changes only the gaps on either side of it, and the three gaps cannot all be fixed by one car: turning B leaves C-D repelling, and turning C leaves A-B repelling. (d) Wrong. If every car is turned round, each gap now has the two other ends facing, and these are again like poles (South facing South, North facing North), so all three pairs still repel. (e) Anywhere: at either end of the train or between any two cars, and either way round, because both ends of an iron bar are attracted by both poles of a magnet.
s: (a) backs: A South, B North, C South, D North
(b) all three pairs repel, like poles facing
(c) two cars, B and D (or A and C), and one is not enough
(d) claim wrong: turning all keeps like poles facing
(e) anywhere, either way round, since iron is attracted by both poles
