Match each set-up in Column I with what is seen in Column II.
Column I: 1. Two matchbox cars with their North poles facing  2. An iron-strip car brought up to a magnet car, either way round  3. A ring magnet staying up above another ring magnet on a pencil  4. Two cars with the North pole of one facing the South pole of the other
Column II: a. The cars run apart  b. The cars move together, but would run apart if one car were turned round  c. The cars move together whichever way the strip car faces  d. Like poles repel and hold the upper one up off the lower

A storage check finds two pairs of bar magnets in a drawer.
Pair P: like poles on the same side, a wooden piece between the magnets, soft-iron pieces across the ends.
Pair Q: unlike poles on the same side, two soft-iron pieces laid between the magnets, a wooden piece across one end.
(a) What single change will make pair P follow the storage rule?
(b) What must be changed in pair Q, and does it need any new pieces?
questions.a: (a) Turn one magnet of pair P round so that unlike poles are on the same side. (b) Pair Q's pieces are in the wrong places: the wooden piece must go between the magnets and the two soft-iron pieces across the ends. No new pieces are needed; the ones it has only have to be swapped.
s: Part (a): turn one magnet round so unlike poles are on the same side
Part (b): swap the pieces, wood between and soft iron across the ends, no new pieces

questions.q: A lab assistant stores two bar magnets side by side with the North pole of one beside the South pole of the other, a wooden strip between them and soft-iron pieces across their ends. She puts the pair in a drawer next to the staff room's TV remote. What still needs to change?
questions.a: The pair must be kept away from the TV remote
o: The pair must be kept away from the TV remote
Like poles must be placed on the same side
The wooden strip must go across the ends
The soft-iron pieces must go between them

questions.q:
The storage rule says to keep magnets in pairs with unlike poles on the same side and to place soft-iron pieces across the ends.
(a) Predict what would happen if two bar magnets were laid side by side with like poles on the same side, and give a reason.
(b) Why can one soft-iron piece cling across the ends of both magnets at once, though one end it touches is a North pole and the other a South pole?
questions.a: (a) The like poles lying side by side would repel each other, so the magnets would push apart (or try to turn round) instead of lying still as a pair. (b) Soft iron is a magnetic material, not a magnet, and both a North pole and a South pole attract iron, so the piece is pulled by both ends at once.
s: Part (a): like poles side by side repel, so the magnets push apart
Part (b): iron is attracted by both poles

questions.q: Arun says, 'Two matchbox cars will run away from each other if the South poles of their magnets face each other, just as they do when the North poles face each other.' Check his claim.
questions.a: Yes, he is right. Like poles repel, and like poles means either the North poles or the South poles of both magnets. South facing South is a pair of like poles, so the cars push apart, just as with North facing North. Only unlike poles (North facing South) would make the cars move together.
s: Verdict: the claim is correct
South-South is a pair of like poles, just as North-North is
Like poles repel, so the cars move apart; only unlike poles would pull them together

questions.q:
A school laboratory keeps 12 bar magnets: ten in a drawer, stored as five pairs, and two on a shelf beside the staff room's TV remote and a teacher's mobile phone. A check of the drawer finds: pairs 1 and 2 have unlike poles on the same side, a wooden piece between the magnets and soft-iron pieces across the ends; pair 3 is complete but has like poles on the same side; pair 4 is correct except that it has no wooden piece; pair 5 has its two soft-iron pieces between the magnets and its wooden piece across one end. The cupboard holds 1 spare wooden piece and 2 spare soft-iron pieces.
(a) Which pairs break the storage rule, and how?
(b) Which of those pairs can be put right without using any spare piece?
(c) After all five pairs are put right, which spare pieces are left, and are they enough to store the two shelf magnets as a sixth pair?
(d) No more pieces can be bought this week. Should the assistant leave the two shelf magnets where they are until a wooden piece arrives, or put them in the drawer now as a pair with unlike poles on the same side and soft-iron pieces across the ends? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Pair 3: like poles on the same side. Pair 4: no wooden piece between the magnets. Pair 5: the pieces are in the wrong places (soft iron between, wood across an end). (b) Pairs 3 and 5: turn one magnet of pair 3 round, and swap pair 5's pieces so that the wooden piece is between the magnets and the two soft-iron pieces are across the ends. (c) Pair 4 uses the spare wooden piece, so 0 wooden and 2 soft-iron pieces are left. A sixth pair needs 1 wooden and 2 soft-iron pieces, so it is one wooden piece short. (d) Put them in the drawer now. On the shelf they break the caution against keeping magnets near mobile phones and remote controls; in the drawer they meet that caution and most of the storage rule (a pair, unlike poles on the same side, soft iron across the ends), and the wooden piece can be added when it arrives.
s: (a) pairs 3, 4 and 5 with the fault in each
(b) pairs 3 and 5 need no spare piece
(c) 2 soft-iron pieces left, one wooden piece short for a sixth pair
(d) move them to the drawer now, weighing the phone and remote caution against the missing wooden piece

questions.q:
Reshma bought three identical metal bars, P, Q and R. Two are magnets and one is plain iron, and she has nothing else to test them with. She first tests P with Q, trying each end of P against each end of Q: they attract every time.
(a) What does this result tell her about P, Q and R?
(b) Next she tests P with R in the same way. What should she conclude if, one way round, they push apart?
(c) What should she conclude if instead P and R attract every time?
(d) Kunal says she should simply look for the pair that pulls together most strongly. Why will this not pick out the magnets?
(e) Using this method, what is the greatest number of pairs Reshma will ever need to test? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Two magnets would push apart one way round, so P and Q cannot both be magnets: one of them is the iron bar, and R must be a magnet. (b) Repulsion happens only between two magnets, so P and R are the magnets and Q is the iron bar. (c) R is a magnet, so if P were a magnet too they would repel one way round; since they only attract, P is the iron bar and Q and R are the magnets. (d) Every pair attracts at some ends, because unlike poles attract and a magnet also attracts both ends of an iron bar; attraction happens in all three pairs, so it cannot pick out the magnets. Only repulsion can. (e) Two. If the first pair repels, those two are the magnets at once. If it only attracts, one more pair (one bar from it with the third bar) settles the answer either way, as in (b) and (c).
s: (a) one of P and Q is iron, so R is a magnet
(b) repulsion: P and R magnets, Q iron
(c) attraction only: P iron, Q and R magnets
(d) attraction occurs in every pair; only repulsion decides
(e) at most two pairs, with reasoning

questions.q:
Three bar magnets lie in a straight line on a table with small gaps between them. From left to right, magnet 1 has ends 1 and 2, magnet 2 has ends 3 and 4, and magnet 3 has ends 5 and 6, so end 2 faces end 3 and end 4 faces end 5. Ends 2 and 3 attract each other, ends 4 and 5 repel each other, and end 5 is a North pole.
(a) What are ends 4 and 6?
(b) What is end 3?
(c) What are ends 1 and 2?
questions.a: (a) End 4 repels the North pole at end 5, so it is a North pole (like poles repel); end 6 is the other end of magnet 3, so it is a South pole. (b) End 3 is the other end of magnet 2, whose end 4 is North, so end 3 is a South pole. (c) End 2 attracts end 3, a South pole, and both are magnet ends, so end 2 is a North pole (unlike poles attract); end 1 is then a South pole.
s: Part (a): end 4 North, end 6 South
Part (b): end 3 South
Part (c): end 2 North, end 1 South

questions.q: Nisha slides a magnet slowly up the outside of a glass of water, and a steel paperclip lying at the bottom follows it to the rim. A plastic button in the same glass stays at the bottom. What explains both results?
questions.a: The effect acts through glass and water; plastic is not attracted
o: The effect acts through glass and water; plastic is not attracted
Glass lets the pull through to the steel clip but blocks it for plastic
The button is heavier, so a pull through water cannot lift it
The water turns the steel clip into a magnet, not the button

questions.q:
Six groups did the compass-and-magnet activity, each recording how far the needle turned from north-south, first with nothing between the magnet and compass and then with a sheet placed between them.
Group 1 (wood): 35 degrees, then 35 degrees.
Group 2 (cardboard): 40 degrees, then 39 degrees.
Group 3 (thin plastic): 30 degrees, then 30 degrees.
Group 4 (thin glass): 35 degrees, then 15 degrees.
Group 5 (thin glass): 32 degrees, then 30 degrees.
Group 6 (thin plastic): 35 degrees, then 28 degrees.
(a) What do Groups 1 to 3 show?
(b) By how many degrees did the reading change for Groups 4, 5 and 6?
(c) What is the most likely reason for Group 4's result? Use the activity's instructions and Group 5's result.
(d) There is time to repeat only one test before the class reports. Should it repeat Group 4's test or Group 6's? Justify.
questions.a: (a) No appreciable change with wood, cardboard or plastic, so the magnetic effect acts through these non-magnetic materials. (b) Group 4: 35 - 15 = 20 degrees; Group 5: 32 - 30 = 2 degrees; Group 6: 35 - 28 = 7 degrees. (c) The magnet or the compass was probably disturbed while the sheet was being placed. The activity requires that they are not moved, and Group 5, using the same thin glass, saw no appreciable change, so the set-up changed, not the effect of the glass. (d) Repeat Group 4's test. Its change of 20 degrees is ten times Group 5's 2 degrees for the same glass, and left unchecked it would lead the class to report, wrongly, that glass blocks the magnet's effect. Group 6's 7 degrees is a smaller change, and the class's conclusion about plastic already rests on Group 3, which saw no change at all, so a repeat of Group 6 would not change what the class reports.
s: (a) no appreciable change; effect acts through non-magnetic materials
(b) 20, 2 and 7 degrees
(c) set-up disturbed, supported by Group 5's glass result
(d) repeat Group 4: largest change, contradicts Group 5, would mislead the report; plastic already settled by Group 3

questions.q: In a fair game, steel balls sit in a maze drawn on a cardboard tray. Players move a magnet under the tray to steer the balls out. Which change would stop the game from working?
questions.a: Using glass marbles instead of the steel balls
o: Using glass marbles instead of the steel balls
Using a thin plastic tray instead of the cardboard one
Using a thin wooden tray instead of cardboard
Drawing a longer, twistier maze on the tray

questions.q: True or False? 'The compass-and-magnet activity tested only wood, cardboard, plastic and glass, so we can say nothing at all about whether a magnet's effect would act through a thin rubber sheet.' Give the verdict and the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Rubber is a non-magnetic material, and the activity led to the conclusion that the magnetic effect can act through non-magnetic materials. So we can predict that the effect will act through a thin rubber sheet, though the prediction should still be checked by testing it.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: rubber is non-magnetic, so the activity's conclusion lets us predict the effect acts through it (to be checked by a test)

(b) Why can the stage be wood?
questions.a: (a) Steel is attracted by a magnet; plastic is non-magnetic and would not be pulled. (b) Wood is non-magnetic and the magnetic effect acts through it, so the magnets below can still pull the clips above.

Part (b): magnetic effect acts through non-magnetic wood

questions.q: Design a simple toy for a younger cousin in which a magnet moves an object without touching it, through a non-magnetic material. Describe it in two or three lines, name the object that moves and the material in between, and explain why it works.
questions.a: E.g. A 'racing beetle': a paper beetle with a steel pin glued under it sits on a thin cardboard race track; a magnet taped to a stick is moved under the track and the beetle races along above. It works because steel is attracted by the magnet and the magnetic effect acts through the non-magnetic cardboard.
s: A toy described clearly
A magnetic moving part and a non-magnetic material in between named

questions.q: With nothing between them, a bar magnet turns a compass needle 28 degrees away from north-south. Without moving either, a thin wooden sheet is stood upright between them. If the chapter's conclusion holds, the needle will now be turned about ___ degrees.

A club is building a 'magnet race' game: a small runner sits on a flat track, and each player moves a magnet under the track to drive the runner along. They can choose the runner from a steel paper clip or a plastic bead, and the track from thin cardboard, a thin plastic sheet or a thin iron sheet.
(a) Which runner must they use, and why?
(b) Which tracks will let the game work, according to the chapter's activity?
(c) Give a reason, from the chapter, for not using the iron track.
(d) A member suggests a plastic bead with a steel pin pushed inside it, because it looks more like a racing ball. Will it work as a runner? Explain.
(e) The game will be played outdoors on a dewy morning, and cardboard goes soft when wet. Which track should the club use? Justify.
questions.a: (a) The steel paper clip: steel is attracted by a magnet, while a plastic bead is non-magnetic and would not move. (b) The thin cardboard and thin plastic tracks: both are non-magnetic, and the magnetic effect acts through non-magnetic materials. (c) The activity tested only non-magnetic sheets, so it gives no support for a track made of iron, which is a magnetic material; the magnet would also be attracted to the iron track itself and cling to its underside. (d) Yes. The steel pin is attracted by the magnet, and the magnetic effect acts through the non-magnetic plastic of the bead, so the bead is carried along. (e) The thin plastic track: it works for the same reason as cardboard, since both are non-magnetic, and unlike cardboard it will not go soft in the dew.
s: (a) steel clip, attracted; plastic bead not
(b) cardboard and plastic, non-magnetic, so the effect acts through
(c) the activity tested only non-magnetic sheets; iron is magnetic and the magnet clings to it
(d) works: steel pin attracted through the non-magnetic plastic
(e) plastic track: works like cardboard and stays firm when wet

questions.q:
Two groups extend the compass-and-magnet activity.
(a) Group A stands a thin glass sheet and a cardboard sheet together between the magnet and the compass, without moving either. Predict what happens to the needle's deflection, and give a reason.
(b) Group B wants to try a thin iron sheet. Can the activity's conclusion be used to predict that result? Explain.
questions.a: (a) No appreciable change in the deflection: glass and cardboard are both non-magnetic, and the magnetic effect acts through non-magnetic materials. (b) No. The conclusion is about non-magnetic materials only; iron is a magnetic material, so the activity tells us nothing about it, and the result would have to be found by testing.
s: Part (a): no appreciable change, since both sheets are non-magnetic
Part (b): no, the conclusion covers only non-magnetic materials and iron is magnetic

questions.q:
A teacher hides a bar magnet inside one of three closed cardboard boxes; the other two hold only wooden blocks. A student slowly moves a compass around the outside of each box.
Box 1: the needle stays pointing north-south.
Box 2: near one side, side X, the needle's North end swings towards the box.
Box 3: the needle stays pointing north-south.
(a) Which box holds the magnet?
(b) Why could the magnet be found without opening the box?
(c) Which pole of the hidden magnet is nearest side X? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Box 2. (b) Cardboard is non-magnetic, and the magnetic effect acts through non-magnetic materials, so the hidden magnet could still deflect the compass needle through the box. (c) The South pole: the needle's North end was pulled closer, and unlike poles attract.
s: Part (a): box 2
Part (b): the magnetic effect acts through the non-magnetic cardboard
Part (c): South pole, since the needle's North end was attracted

questions.q: Differentiate between 'a magnet attracting cardboard' and 'a magnet acting through cardboard'. Which of the two actually happens?
questions.a: Attracting cardboard would mean the cardboard itself is pulled towards the magnet, which needs a magnetic material. Acting through cardboard means the magnet's effect passes through the cardboard to reach something magnetic beyond it. Only the second happens, because cardboard is non-magnetic.
s: The two ideas correctly contrasted
Only acting through happens, because cardboard is non-magnetic

questions.q:
Ananya stands a thin sheet of an unknown grey material upright between a bar magnet and a compass needle, taking care not to move either, and the needle's deflection changes a lot.
(a) What can she infer about the sheet, using the activity's conclusion?
(b) How could she check this with the magnet alone?
questions.a: (a) The activity found no appreciable change for non-magnetic sheets. Since the set-up was not disturbed and the deflection changed a lot, the sheet is probably not a non-magnetic material, so the activity's conclusion does not cover it. (b) Bring the magnet near the sheet by itself: if the sheet is attracted towards the magnet, it is a magnetic material.
s: Part (a): the sheet is probably not non-magnetic, so the conclusion does not apply to it
Part (b): test whether the sheet itself is attracted by the magnet

questions.q:
Class 6B runs a magnet-maze stall at the school fair. Each game uses a cardboard tray with a maze drawn on it, steel balls and a bar magnet that players move underneath. They buy one tray for Rs 40, 12 steel balls at Rs 5 each and 2 bar magnets at Rs 70 each. They charge Rs 10 a game and 46 games are played.
(a) Why does moving the magnet under the tray make the balls move?
(b) What did the stall's materials cost?
(c) How much profit did the stall make?
(d) After the stall closes, the cardboard tray is soft and torn, and the club needs a tray for next year's fair. The club must keep Rs 150 of its profit for next year's steel balls and magnets. With the rest, can it buy a thin plastic tray (Rs 90), or should it buy a new cardboard tray (Rs 40)? Justify using the chapter and your numbers.
questions.a: (a) Steel is attracted by the magnet, and the magnetic effect acts through the non-magnetic cardboard. (b) 40 + 12 x 5 + 2 x 70 = 40 + 60 + 140 = Rs 240. (c) 46 x 10 = Rs 460 collected; profit Rs 460 - Rs 240 = Rs 220. (d) A new cardboard tray. After keeping Rs 150, the club has Rs 220 - Rs 150 = Rs 70, which is less than the Rs 90 a plastic tray costs. A thin plastic tray would work, because plastic is non-magnetic and the magnetic effect acts through it, but the cardboard tray works the same way and its Rs 40 fits within the Rs 70.
s: (a) steel attracted, effect acts through non-magnetic cardboard
(d) cardboard tray, since only Rs 70 is free, noting plastic would also work

questions.q: After the activity with wood, cardboard, thin plastic and thin glass sheets, Dhruv says, 'So a magnet's effect will pass through any material at all, of any thickness.' Check his claim.
questions.a: Partly right. The activity does show that the magnetic effect acts through non-magnetic materials, since none of the four sheets made an appreciable change. But only these four materials, as thin sheets, were tested, so the activity gives no evidence about every material or about any thickness; his conclusion goes beyond what was observed.
s: Verdict: partly right
Correct part: the effect acts through the non-magnetic sheets tested
Overreach: only four materials, thin sheets, were tested

questions.q:
Kiran wrote this plan to test whether a magnet's effect passes through wood:
1. Put the compass on a table and bring a bar magnet near it; note how far the needle turns.
2. Lay the wooden sheet flat on the table beside the compass.
3. Move the magnet a little closer so that the sheet fits between the magnet and the compass.
4. Note how far the needle turns now.
5. Conclude: 'The needle turned more, so wood adds to a magnet's pull.'
Say what is wrong in steps 2, 3 and 5 and correct each. Then say how the results for wood, cardboard, thin plastic and thin glass should be recorded, and what result and conclusion the activity leads to.
questions.a: Step 2: the sheet must stand upright, perpendicular to the table, between the magnet and the compass, not lie flat beside them. Step 3: the magnet and the compass must not be disturbed; moving the magnet changes the set-up, so any change could be due to the move and not the wood. Step 5: the extra turning came from moving the magnet closer, not from the wood, so the conclusion is not supported. Record each material and the observation in a table (material placed between, observation). The activity shows no appreciable change in deflection for any of these sheets, so the magnetic effect can act through non-magnetic materials.
s: Step 2 corrected: sheet upright between magnet and compass
Step 3 corrected: magnet and compass not disturbed, with reason
Step 5 corrected: the change came from moving the magnet, not the wood
Results recorded in a table of material and observation
No appreciable change; the effect acts through non-magnetic materials
